questions.prompt: An integrity-constraint violation prevents a transaction from completing. How does the lecture classify it?
options: A logical error in the transaction
A system crash that loses all RAM state
A media failure that destroys nonvolatile storage
A DBMS software failure rather than a transaction-level logical condition
questions.explanation: A constraint violation is a logical reason to abort. It does not mean that the storage hardware has failed.

questions.prompt: The DBMS aborts a transaction to break a deadlock. What kind of failure is this?
options: A media failure because a transaction loses its locks
An internal-state error leading to transaction failure
A system crash requiring rollback of committed transactions
No recovery is needed because there was no power failure
questions.explanation: A deadlock victim still needs rollback and undo. Recovery mechanisms are needed for more than power failures.

questions.prompt: What does the lecture's fail-stop assumption for a system crash preserve?
options: All RAM contents
The guarantee that no transaction was in progress
The contents of nonvolatile storage
The guarantee that every dirty page reached disk before power failed
questions.explanation: This model allows volatile state to be lost while durable storage remains intact. It does not assume that RAM survives a crash.

questions.prompt: Both data disks and the log are destroyed, leaving no local recovery information. What is needed?
options: Analysis of the log that was also lost
Reading the buffer pool after RAM has lost its contents
Rolling back only the last transaction to reconstruct the entire database
A surviving backup or replica elsewhere
questions.explanation: WAL-based recovery requires a surviving WAL. If both the data and log are lost, recovery must rely on a copy that still exists.

questions.prompt: What activities does crash recovery involve?
options: Preparation during normal processing and recovery after failure
Work only after a crash, with no recovery information stored beforehand
Flushing data pages only after detecting that power has already failed
Restarting the process without examining the log or transaction state
questions.explanation: Recovery information must be saved before a failure so it is available afterward. Restarting alone cannot reconstruct lost state.

questions.prompt: What does STEAL permit?
options: A requester may bypass another transaction's lock
Pages containing uncommitted updates may be flushed to nonvolatile storage
Every dirty page must reach disk before commit
No page modified by a transaction may be evicted
questions.explanation: STEAL is a buffer-replacement and flushing policy, not permission to bypass concurrency control. FORCE concerns flushing requirements at commit.

questions.prompt: What does NO-FORCE mean?
options: Data pages are never written to disk
Log flushing at commit is forbidden
Not every modified data page must reach disk before commit
Only read-only transactions may commit
questions.explanation: NO-FORCE removes the requirement to flush every data page at commit. It permits later flushing and does not waive the log's durability requirements.

questions.prompt: Why does STEAL require UNDO support?
options: Committed changes may be missing from disk data pages
STEAL requires deleting all update logs before commit
STEAL forbids storing update before-images
Disk may contain changes from a transaction that later aborts
questions.explanation: For example B=7 changes to B=3 without commit, and STEAL flushes B=3. If the transaction aborts, the disk contains unfinished work. UNDO needs the information that restores 7; REDOing 3 would preserve the wrong effect.

questions.prompt: Why does NO-FORCE require REDO support?
options: A crash can lose committed updates that exist only in RAM
Every transaction must be undone at commit
NO-FORCE permits deleting the log immediately after updating RAM
Only uncommitted dirty pages can be lost in a crash
questions.explanation: For example T1 commits A=10 while disk still has A=12. Power loss removes RAM. Because T1 already committed, restoring 12 would lose accepted work; REDO uses the durable log to reconstruct 10. NO-FORCE does not waive durable-log requirements.

questions.prompt: What limitation of NO-STEAL + FORCE is discussed?
options: It always gives the fastest runtime
It requires buffering uncommitted pages and incurs flushing work at commit
Crashes during a multi-page flush need no consideration
Every uncommitted page may be evicted
questions.explanation: NO-STEAL requires sufficient buffer space, and FORCE increases commit-time writing. These policies do not automatically make a multi-page flush atomic.

questions.prompt: What should a recovery log contain for an update?
options: Only a transaction ID and object name, with no way to reconstruct or reverse the update
Only a COMMIT record, with all update information omitted
Enough information for undo and redo as required by the chosen policies
Only an after-image, even when STEAL requires UNDO
questions.explanation: Recovery must be able to reverse or reconstruct effects. An identity or query plan alone does not determine the values to restore.

questions.prompt: Why can logging be more efficient than flushing scattered data pages during normal processing?
options: Every log record requires its own flush, so I/O can never be grouped
Logging means data pages never need writing to storage
Every update requires copying the entire database into the log
The log is written sequentially and can pack many small updates into one page
questions.explanation: Compact sequential logging reduces random I/O. It neither removes every cost nor requires copying the whole database for each update.

questions.prompt: T changes A from 14 to 9. What does a log record containing old=14 and new=9 support?
options: UNDO restores 14, and REDO writes 9
UNDO writes 9, and REDO restores 14
Both UNDO and REDO set A to 14
Both UNDO and REDO set A to 9
questions.explanation: The before-image supports undo, and the after-image supports redo. Reversing these roles reconstructs the wrong state.

questions.prompt: What goes wrong if the recovery log exists only in RAM when power fails?
options: A transaction ID makes a RAM log stable storage
Recovery information can be lost alongside unflushed data pages
Every RAM log can automatically be recovered from a page that was also lost
A BEGIN record in RAM is enough to redo every update
questions.explanation: Logging relies on durable recovery information. Log records that have not been persisted do not survive power loss merely because they are in RAM.

questions.prompt: What does it mean to separate the log file from the actual data?
options: The log is the only copy of data pages and contains no update history
Every log record must occupy the same page as the data it describes
The log contains history and recovery information, while data pages contain database state
Data pages never need flushing because a log exists
questions.explanation: Separating these roles allows sequential log writes and data-page flushing when needed. A log is not an index and does not make data immutable.

questions.prompt: Before flushing a dirty page P, what does WAL require?
options: Every running transaction must commit together
A BEGIN record in RAM is sufficient
P must be flushed first so the log can record its disk value
Log records for the relevant updates to P must already be durable
questions.explanation: Recovery information must be durable before the page whose effects it may need to undo or redo. A BEGIN record in RAM is insufficient.

questions.prompt: When may the system report a successful transaction commit under the lecture's WAL rules?
options: When all of its log records, including COMMIT, are on nonvolatile storage
Immediately after COMMIT is appended to the in-memory log
Only when all data pages have been flushed under FORCE
As soon as update records are durable, even if COMMIT is not
questions.explanation: A durable log allows WAL to work with NO-FORCE. Every data page need not be flushed, but a COMMIT record present only in RAM is insufficient.

questions.prompt: A data page with a new value is flushed before its update log is durable, and a crash follows. What is the risk?
options: None; a durable data page automatically means its transaction committed
The information needed to undo an uncommitted change may be missing
The old value can always be reconstructed from the new disk value
Knowing the transaction's name is enough to undo every update
questions.explanation: This violates log-before-page ordering. Storage contains an effect without the history needed to reverse it; a SELECT cannot reconstruct that missing history.

questions.prompt: Disk has A=5. T commits A=11, with its log and COMMIT durable, but its data page is not flushed before a crash. How can A be recovered?
options: UNDO to 5 while still treating T as successful
It cannot be recovered because the data page was not flushed
REDO from the log to obtain 11
Discard the update because the data disk is the only source of truth
questions.explanation: The durable transaction log contains the information needed to reconstruct the change. This is why NO-FORCE can still provide durability.

questions.prompt: Which sequence respects WAL before writing a page and acknowledging commit?
options: Flush page → append update log → report commit
Append COMMIT in RAM → report success → flush log later
Report commit → discard log → flush page
Append log in RAM → flush update log → flush data page → flush COMMIT log → report success
questions.explanation: Update-log durability comes before its data-page flush; durability of the transaction log through COMMIT comes before the success message. This option is one valid ordering, not a requirement that every data page always be flushed before commit: NO-FORCE may defer that page write.

questions.prompt: What is the order of the three ARIES phases in the lecture?
options: Analysis → Redo → Undo
Undo → Analysis → Redo
Analysis → Undo → Redo
Redo → Analysis → Undo
questions.explanation: ARIES first reconstructs recovery state, then repeats history, and finally rolls back uncommitted transactions. It does not simply commit every transaction after a crash.

questions.prompt: What information does analysis identify?
options: Only committed transactions, ignoring active transactions
Active transactions and dirty pages at the crash
Only clean data pages, because dirty pages recover themselves
Only COMMIT order, without examining pages or update logs
questions.explanation: Analysis builds the information needed for subsequent recovery work. A list of schema objects alone is insufficient.

questions.prompt: Can ARIES redo repeat effects from a transaction that will subsequently be undone?
options: No; redo considers only committed transactions in every algorithm
Yes, and that transaction must then commit
Yes, because ARIES repeats history before undoing losers
No; redo applies only to reads
questions.explanation: ARIES reconstructs history, including loser effects, before undoing them. Repeating an effect does not authorize the loser to commit.

questions.prompt: Which transactions are handled by undo after redo?
options: Every committed transaction, because redo has repeated it
Only transactions with unflushed dirty pages, excluding losers whose pages reached disk
Only the last transaction started before the crash
Transactions that had not committed before the crash
questions.explanation: For the ordinary single-node transactions in this question, undo removes unfinished work while committed work is retained. Lecture 22 adds an important boundary: a distributed participant with durable PREPARE alone is in doubt and must resolve its shared decision before being treated as a loser.

questions.prompt: T1 commits A=8; T2 writes B=4 without committing before a crash. What is the correct recovery goal?
options: Retain T1's effects and remove T2's effects
Retain both because every executed UPDATE must be durable
Remove both because a crash cancels committed transactions too
Retain only transactions whose data pages were flushed, regardless of COMMIT
questions.explanation: Durability preserves T1, while atomicity removes T2. Redo may temporarily repeat T2's effects, but undo must remove them before recovery's final result.
